title: Expressions with bring and take
subtitle: bring up, bring about, take after, take for granted
summary: Use the most common phrasal verbs and fixed expressions built on bring and take, and say what each of them means.

lesson.heading: Phrasal verbs with bring
rows: lower; or destroy, remove from power

lesson.heading: bring in sentences
lesson.text: Note that **bring down** has two quite different meanings: you bring down prices or taxes, and you also bring down a government.

examples.text: My father's parents **brought** him **up** in the country.
Don't give up. I'm sure you'll **bring** it **off** in the end.
Cold winds always **bring on** her cough.
The strike **brought about** a change of government.
Ford Motors are **bringing out** an interesting new model in the spring.
I hope they don't **bring back** capital punishment.
Keep trying to persuade him and you'll **bring** him **round** to your point of view.

lesson.heading: Phrasal verbs with take
rows: leave the ground; start to improve; imitate
start doing a job someone else was doing

lesson.heading: take in sentences
lesson.text: **Take off** is the busiest of these: a plane takes off, sales take off, and a comedian takes off a famous person. The context makes the meaning clear.

examples.text: Doesn't he **take after** his father! They even sound the same.
It's hard to **take in** his lectures - he speaks in such an abstract way.
She was completely **taken in** by him and agreed to give him all her money.
Sales have really **taken off** now - we should make a good profit this year.
We'll have to **take on** more staff if we're to **take on** more work.
She **took to** him at once and they soon became close friends.

lesson.heading: Fixed expressions with bring
rows: reach a point where changes have to be made

lesson.text: Take it for granted that ... = assume it, but take someone for granted = fail to appreciate them. Same words, very different feeling.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrasal verb with its more formal equivalent.
The school reforms which plan to bring ___ a more traditional style of exams are generally unpopular.
exercises.explanation: Bring back = re-introduce something that existed before.

exercises.prompt: The bumpy journey brought ___ labour and the baby was born on the bus.
exercises.explanation: Bring on = cause something to start.

exercises.prompt: I think the strikes will bring ___ some changes in management.
He won't agree to it for me, but she can always bring him ___.
exercises.explanation: Bring someone round = persuade them to your point of view.

exercises.prompt: Complete: If anyone can bring it ___, he can.
exercises.explanation: Bring something off = succeed in doing something difficult.

exercises.prompt: She brought ___ six children all on her own.
exercises.explanation: Bring up a child = raise a child.

exercises.prompt: Today's newspaper has brought ___ some fascinating information about the President.
exercises.explanation: Bring something to light = reveal it.

exercises.prompt: The situation was brought ___ when the union called for a strike.
exercises.explanation: Bring matters to a head = reach the point where changes have to be made.

exercises.prompt: The view from the top of the hill ___ my breath away.
exercises.explanation: Take someone's breath away = amaze them.

exercises.statement: He took advantage of her weakness at the time and she gave it to him.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Take advantage of someone = unfairly use your superiority over them.

exercises.statement: You shouldn't take anyone or anything to light.
exercises.explanation: You shouldn't take anyone or anything for granted. Take for granted = assume it will always be the same.

exercises.prompt: Does each expression begin with bring or take?
Put the words in order. (The story happens in Mexico.)
exercises.answer: The story takes place in Mexico
